extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, performers, producers, and students/historians of television comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, production-oriented criteria and lessons for writing, performing, and producing television sketch and late-night comedy, drawn from Robert Smigel's career and interview commentary. Covers creative intent, room dynamics, character work, standards & practices, and live-vs-taped considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Intent matters. It matters in crime and it matters in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comedic material by its intended purpose and target — e.g., Smigel describes 'Christmastime for the Jews' and other parodies as intended to make fun of racists or poke at specific targets. Use intent to distinguish malicious content from satire meant to criticize. Example: 'intent should matter in comedy - if it matters in crime, it matters in comedy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Target selection / punch_up principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose appropriate targets for satire and parody so the joke critiques harmful behavior or power rather than punching down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel frames certain animated pieces as 'making fun of racists' — the example 'Journey to the Disney Vault' uses parody to lampoon racist attitudes. When evaluating jokes, consider who is being targeted and whether the satire 'punches up.'

rubrics_metrics.name: First read-through as a key testing moment
rubrics_metrics.description: The first read-through at SNL is crucial for discovering what lands and what bombs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel emphasizes the importance of the first read-through in the writers' room as a diagnostic: even very funny sketches can fail in read-through, so use it to iterate, re-time, and reshape material before taping or going live.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live audience unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the funniest sketches in the room may bomb in front of a live audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because SNL is live, sketches may succeed in rehearsal but fail live; evaluate robustness of material across settings and be prepared to adjust. Consider audience dynamics, timing, and delivery under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium matters: live vs. pre-taped
rubrics_metrics.description: Live broadcast is a different medium than pre-taped; the live format changes what works and how material must be written and performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel notes SNL's special nature as a live broadcast. When producing or judging comedy, consider the constraints and opportunities of the medium (immediacy, audience reaction, risk of improvisation) and write accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints can enhance comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations from Standards & Practices or other constraints can make bits funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: the 'Masturbating Bear' bit was funnier due to limitations imposed by Standards & Practices. Constraints force creativity — use them to inspire tighter, more inventive comedic choices rather than seeing them only as censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for controversy and institutional pushback
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversial sketches may be pulled, not re-aired, or trigger network notes and backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel recounts 'Conspiracy Theory Rock!' getting notes from NBC and later being pulled; The Dana Carvey Show pilot caused thousands of complaints. When producing provocative comedy, expect institutional review and potential fallout; weigh the benefits and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance scripted material and improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful remote or character bits often mix pre-written lines with improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On 'Triumph' sketches Smigel explains how much is pre-written and how much is improvised. Evaluate how a bit will function if performers must improvise—and plan anchor beats while leaving room for spontaneous moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character design and props support performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A memorable comedy character needs distinct traits, physical props, and a clear persona (e.g., Triumph's cigar, bow tie, deadpan stare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel details Triumph's visual and vocal hallmarks; when creating characters, define props/looks and vocal choices that enable the performer to inhabit the role and generate material consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catchphrases and repeated motifs strengthen recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Catchphrases (like 'da Bears') and recurring motifs anchor sketches and create audience recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel highlights 'Da Bears' and other catchphrases as durable elements. Use repetition carefully to build familiarity without becoming stale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to performer and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Different performers and formats require different comedic styles; a dry, conversational joke may 'kill' in a read-through yet be hard to pull off live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel contrasts his dry style with performers who 'go small' (Kristen Wiig) and stresses tailoring material to a performer's strengths and the venue. Evaluate whether material fits the performer's instincts and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the rhythm / 'music' of an impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful impressions capture rhythm and musicality ('finding the music') rather than only surface mimicry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel explains working with Dana Carvey on finding 'the music' in impressions. When evaluating impressions, listen for timing, cadence, and internal rhythm that make the impersonation expressive and funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go to the 'stress' in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comedy often 'goes right to where the stress is' — targeting the emotional or high-pressure kernel of a situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel describes wanting to go to the stress in humor for Conan's show. Use emotional tension or discomfort as fertile ground for comedy, while managing taste and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and writers' room dynamics shape material
rubrics_metrics.description: Endorsements, complementary writers, and room chemistry are critical to getting sketches on air and making them better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel references endorsements that helped him return to SNL, and the influence of writers like Jim Downey and Al Franken. Evaluate not just the draft but how it plays in the room and who supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting matters — match material to the right performer
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting the right performer can set the tone and timing of a sketch (e.g., choosing Phil Hartman or getting authentic accents to set a 'metronome').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel recounts casting choices for 'Bill Swerski's Superfans' and how a more authentic accent set the pace. When producing or judging, consider whether the cast can realize the material as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy enables risk-taking and distinctive voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Having autonomy over a segment or series enables a creator to pursue a distinct voice and riskier material (Smigel's 'TV Funhouse' cartoons had such autonomy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel notes the autonomy he had with 'TV Funhouse' which allowed edgier satire. Creative control can produce unique, sometimes controversial work — factor creator autonomy into expectations for style and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should prioritize comedy over partisan skewering
rubrics_metrics.description: Political satire should focus on the comedy rather than merely skewering one side of the political spectrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel describes Jim Downey's preference for focusing on comedy rather than political partisanship. Evaluate political sketches on comedic merit first and whether they provide insight or merely partisan attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody leverages familiarity and may subvert expectation/emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective parody uses audience familiarity with the original (e.g., Peanuts specials) and can generate unexpected genuine emotional responses by subverting that form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel's Peanuts parody surprised him when the audience reacted with genuine emotion. When crafting or assessing parody, consider how faithful framing plus subversion will land emotionally and comedically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career and craft development: practice, influences, and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing a comedic voice involves early influences, persistent practice, and participation in institutions (e.g., Second City, writers' rooms, contests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel traces his path from stand-up contests to Second City to SNL. For emerging comedians, evaluate progress by growth in craft, exposure to varied influences, and experience in collaborative comedy settings.
